posts.title: Tire pressure: where to find the right number and when to check
posts.body:
The right pressure for your tires is the number your vehicle maker sets, not the number printed on the tire. The sidewall shows a maximum, and FuelEconomy.gov says not to inflate to it.

Where to find it: a label on the driver's door edge or door pillar, sometimes in the glove box, and in the owner's manual. It's usually listed in both psi and kPa. The UK Highway Code adds that pressure should match the maker's figure for the load you're carrying.

When to check: NHTSA recommends at least once a month, spare included. The Highway Code says weekly and before a long journey. Check when the tires are cold, after the car has been parked for about three hours, because warm tires give misleading readings.

Why it matters: NHTSA links low pressure to flats, blowouts and tread separation, as well as uneven wear and shorter tire life. FuelEconomy.gov estimates gas mileage drops about 0.2% for every 1 psi below the recommended pressure.

About the warning light: US passenger cars, light trucks and vans have had tire pressure monitoring (TPMS) since the 2008 model year. It only lights up when a tire is significantly low, so it doesn't replace a monthly check. If the light flashes for a minute or so and then stays on, the system itself may have a fault.

Log each check in Checkpit and set a monthly reminder so it doesn't slip.

Sources:
- NHTSA, Tires: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/tires
- GOV.UK, The Highway Code, Annex 6: Vehicle maintenance, safety and security: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-highway-code/annex-6-vehicle-maintenance-safety-and-security
- FuelEconomy.gov, Keeping Your Vehicle in Shape: https://www.fueleconomy.gov/feg/maintain.jsp

posts.title: Tire tread depth: legal limits and how to check
posts.body:
Every tire reaches a point where it's worn out, and the limit depends on where you drive.

United States: NHTSA advises replacing tires when the tread is down to 2/32 of an inch (about 1.6 mm).

United Kingdom: cars, light vans and light trailers need at least 1.6 mm of tread across the central three-quarters of the tread, all the way around the tire.

Victoria, Australia: tires need at least 1.5 mm in all principal grooves, and the tread must not wear down to where a wear indicator touches the road. Elsewhere, check your own state or provincial road authority.

How to check: most tires have tread wear indicators, small raised bars inside the grooves. When the tread is level with them, NHTSA says it's time to replace the tire. In the US, NHTSA also describes the penny test: put a penny into a groove with Lincoln's head upside down and facing you. If you can see the top of his head, replace the tire.

While you're there: look for deep cuts, cracks and bulges. Victoria's rules say a tire with damage like that must come off the car, and repairs are only allowed in the tread area, not the sidewall or shoulder. NHTSA suggests checking tread at the same time as pressure, at least once a month.

Note each check in Checkpit so you can see how quickly your tires are wearing.

Sources:
- NHTSA, Tires: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/tires
- GOV.UK, The Highway Code, Annex 6: Vehicle maintenance, safety and security: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-highway-code/annex-6-vehicle-maintenance-safety-and-security

posts.title: Oil changes: how to find the right interval for your car
posts.body:
There's no single oil change interval that fits every car. The right one comes from your vehicle maker, and it can change with how you drive.

Start with the owner's manual or a dealer. They give the interval and the oil type your engine needs. California's used oil program notes that some engines require synthetic oil only.

Oil life monitors: some cars have a monitor that tells you when an oil change is due. If yours does, it's the most direct signal you have.

Normal or severe driving: the maker's standard interval assumes normal driving. California's guidance lists conditions that may mean changing oil more often: very cold or very hot weather, towing or hauling heavy loads, lots of trips under five miles, and a lot of idling or stop-and-go traffic. If any of these is part of a typical week for you, check whether your manual has a separate severe-service schedule.

Use the right grade: FuelEconomy.gov says using the oil grade the maker recommends can improve gas mileage by 1% to 2%, and using a heavier grade than specified, such as 10W-30 in an engine designed for 5W-30, can lower it by 1% to 2%. It also suggests looking for "Energy Conserving" in the API symbol on the bottle.

Log each oil change in Checkpit with the mileage. The app's oil change reminder starts at 6 months or 5,000 miles (8,000 km); change it to match your manual.

Sources:
- CalRecycle (State of California), Check Your Number: https://www2.calrecycle.ca.gov/UsedOil/changeinterval
- FuelEconomy.gov, Keeping Your Vehicle in Shape: https://www.fueleconomy.gov/feg/maintain.jsp

posts.title: Brake fluid: what it does and when to change it
posts.body:
Brake fluid turns a push on the pedal into stopping power. Pressing the pedal sends fluid from the master cylinder to the pistons that squeeze the pads against the brake discs.

Why it wears out: brake fluid attracts moisture. AAA's brake care guide says not to leave the reservoir open and to throw out spare fluid from an opened bottle. Tesla's owner instructions also say to use only new fluid from a sealed container, because old or opened fluid absorbs moisture and reduces braking performance. Fluid also darkens with age.

When to change it: AAA's general guideline is about every two years, and it notes some makers say every two to three years. Your owner's manual has the interval for your car.

How to check it: the reservoir usually sits on top of the master cylinder at the back of the engine bay, on the driver's side. The level should be between the marks. New fluid is clear to tan; dark fluid is a sign it needs a service. Use only the type your manual names. Some makers, such as Tesla, tell owners not to top it up themselves, so check the manual first.

Warning signs: a level near or below the lower mark, or having to add fluid often, can mean a leak or worn pads. AAA advises having the brakes inspected as soon as possible. If the red brake warning light comes on while driving, brake gently and stop when it's safe.

Brake fluid damages paint, so wipe up spills right away.

Add a Brake fluid reminder in Checkpit and set it to repeat at your manual's interval.

Sources:
- AAA (Your AAA Network), How to Care for Your Car Brakes: https://magazine.northeast.aaa.com/daily/life/cars-trucks/care-for-car-brakes/

posts.title: Car battery: how long it lasts and when to test it
posts.body:
Most car batteries last three to five years, according to both AAA and Australia's NRMA. Climate matters: AAA says a battery may last five years or more in cooler places but around three years in hot ones, because heat speeds up wear.

What shortens battery life:
- Mostly short trips, which don't let the battery fully recharge (NRMA adds that running the air conditioning or infotainment on those trips makes it harder)
- Long periods parked, since batteries slowly discharge
- A loose hold-down that lets the battery vibrate
- Letting it go completely flat, even if it's recharged afterward
- A fault in the charging system

Signs it may be failing: slow engine cranking, clicking when you turn the key, the battery or charging warning light, dim headlights at idle, frequent jump-starts, a rotten-egg smell, or a swollen case. Some batteries fail with no warning at all.

When to test: AAA suggests checking the battery and cable connections at every oil change and having the battery tested every year once it's three years old. NRMA also recommends a battery health check after three years. At about five years, a battery is near the end of its usual life.

Keep the terminals clean and tight and the hold-down secure. When replacing it, match the type, group number and CCA or Ah rating your vehicle calls for.

Log the battery's install date in Checkpit and add a Battery reminder for a yearly test from year three.

Sources:
- AAA, How Long Do Car Batteries Last: https://www.aaa.com/autorepair/articles/how-long-do-car-batteries-last
- AAA, When to Replace Your Car's Battery: https://www.aaa.com/autorepair/articles/when-to-replace-your-cars-battery

posts.title: Dashboard warning lights: what the colors mean
posts.body:
Most cars color-code their warning lights. Symbols vary, so your owner's manual is the final word; National Highways (England) suggests checking it or asking the maker about anything specific to your car.

Red: a possibly serious or dangerous problem. The RAC's advice is to stop as soon as it's safe and get the car checked.
Amber or yellow: something needs checking soon. Less urgent, but don't ignore it.
Green, white or blue: information only, such as a system being on.
National Highways advises not starting a trip with a red or amber light showing.

Lights that come on briefly when you start the car are normal. One that stays on is the one to act on.

Red lights to take seriously (RAC guidance):
- Brake: pull over safely, keep speed low and avoid sudden braking.
- Oil: stop when safe, switch off and check the oil level. If the level is fine, don't drive on; the pump may be at fault.
- Engine temperature: stop and let the engine cool before checking coolant.
- Battery or charging: the car may lose power suddenly, so get it checked.
- Airbag: the airbags may not work in a crash. Get it checked right away.

Amber lights: tire pressure (check pressures when safe), ABS on its own (normal braking should still work, but get it checked; with the brake light too, stop), and engine management (get it checked as soon as you can).

On a highway or motorway, don't stop in a live lane unless you must. If you can drive safely, head for the next exit or service area.

When a light leads to a repair, log it in Checkpit with the date and mileage.

Sources:
- RAC, Dashboard warning lights guide: https://www.rac.co.uk/drive/advice/know-how/car-dashboard-warning-lights-meaning/
- National Highways, Dashboard warning lights: what you need to know: https://nationalhighways.co.uk/road-safety/dashboard-warning-lights/

posts.title: Vehicle recalls: how to check if your car has one
posts.body:
A recall means the maker has found a safety problem with a vehicle or part. Checking is free and takes a few minutes.

Find your VIN: it's 17 characters. NHTSA says to look at the lower left of the windshield; it's also on your registration and may be on your insurance card.

US: enter your VIN at nhtsa.gov/recalls. It shows unrepaired recalls from about the past 15 years. NHTSA's free SaferCar app can alert you to new recalls for a vehicle you've saved.
Canada: Transport Canada's database lists recalls issued in Canada since 1970, and it suggests looking up your VIN on the maker's website. The Government of Canada recalls and safety alerts app also shows vehicle recalls.
UK: GOV.UK's recall check uses your registration number, or the make, model and year.
Australia: search the federal Vehicle Recalls website (vehiclerecalls.gov.au), where you can also sign up for email alerts.

Is the fix free? NHTSA tells owners to contact a dealer to fix the recalled part for free. Transport Canada says makers almost always repair recalls free of charge, and GOV.UK says you usually won't pay for repairs or parts.

Registering your car with the maker is one way to get recall notices directly, according to Transport Canada. GOV.UK says not to drive a vehicle with a serious safety defect.

After a recall repair, log it in Checkpit with the date and mileage so it stays in the car's history.

Sources:

- Transport Canada, Stay informed about recalls of vehicles, tires and child car seats: https://tc.canada.ca/en/road-transportation/defects-recalls-vehicles-tires-child-car-seats/stay-informed-about-recalls-vehicles-tires-child-car-seats

posts.title: Engine coolant: how to check it and when to look closer
posts.body:
Coolant (antifreeze) is mixed with water to keep the engine from overheating in summer and freezing in winter. It also protects the cooling system from rust and corrosion.

Check it cold. The AA says to wait at least 30 minutes after switching off, longer if the engine has overheated, and not to open the cap until the engine has fully cooled, because hot coolant is under pressure and can scald. Find the see-through expansion tank (your manual shows where it is). The level should be between the min and max marks. The AA suggests a quick look every couple of weeks.

Topping up: use only the coolant type your vehicle calls for. The AA notes that different types don't mix well, many need a 50/50 mix with water, and some makers use a pre-mixed coolant you shouldn't add anything to. Plain water is for emergencies only, since coolant that's too weak can freeze in winter. Never pour antifreeze into the washer, brake or power steering reservoirs.

When to look closer: the AA says modern cooling systems shouldn't need topping up between services, so a dropping level means a visit to a shop. Watch for wet or white stains on hoses, cool air from the heater on the hot setting, and the coolant warning light (amber usually means low level; red means overheating).

Replacing it: coolant turns acidic over time and loses its rust protection. AAA says that once a car reaches 75,000 miles, the coolant should be tested at regular intervals, and if the test is fine, no flush is needed. Your owner's manual has the replacement interval.

Add a Coolant reminder in Checkpit and log each test or change with the mileage.

Sources:
- The AA, How to check your engine coolant and top it up: https://www.theaa.com/breakdown-cover/advice/how-to-check-your-engine-coolant

posts.title: Winter car checklist: what to check before the cold
posts.body:
Cold weather is hard on cars. Here is what NHTSA and Public Safety Canada (with the CAA) suggest checking before winter.

Battery: cold reduces battery power, and engines need more of it to start. NHTSA suggests having a mechanic check the battery, charging system and belts.

Tires: pressure drops as it gets colder. Check it at least once a month with the tires cold, and fill to the number on the driver's door label or in the manual, not the one on the tire. NHTSA says tread should be at least 2/32 inch on every tire, and to check the spare too. Winter tires add grip on cold roads.

Wipers and washer fluid: fill up with winter washer fluid (Public Safety Canada suggests one rated to -40°C, plus a spare jug), replace blades that streak, and make sure the defrosters work.

Coolant and lights: check the coolant level and that it meets the maker's specification, and look for leaks. Check headlights, brake lights, turn signals and hazard lights.

Fuel: NHTSA says to keep the tank close to full; Public Safety Canada says at least half full. For electric and hybrid cars, NHTSA suggests keeping the battery charged; plugging in overnight helps.

Emergency kit: ice scraper and snow brush, small shovel, sand or cat litter for traction, jumper cables, flashlight, warning lights or flares, blankets, first aid kit, water, snacks and a phone charger.

If you get stuck, keep the exhaust pipe clear of snow and run the engine only now and then to stay warm, never for long with the windows up.

Log your pre-winter check in Checkpit and set reminders for battery tests and tire changes.

Sources:
- NHTSA, Winter Weather Driving Tips: https://www.nhtsa.gov/winter-driving-tips
- Public Safety Canada (with CAA), Winter Driving: https://getprepared.gc.ca/cnt/rsrcs/sfttps/tp201002-en.aspx

posts.title: Wiper blades and washer fluid: when to replace and refill
posts.body:
Clear glass is a safety basic, and in Great Britain it's a legal one too: GOV.UK says a car with a windscreen must have working automatic wipers and a washer, kept in efficient working order.

When to replace blades: AAA says most mechanics and makers recommend new blades every six to twelve months. Climate, where you park, how often you use them and the type of blade all affect how long they last.

Signs they're worn: streaks or smears that get in the way, squeaking, skipping across the glass (cold can harden the rubber), and cracked, torn or frayed rubber. Check the manual or measure the old blades to get the right size.

Washer fluid: before winter, NHTSA suggests filling the reservoir with winter de-icing fluid and checking the defrosters, and notes that heavy-duty winter blades help where snow and ice are common. Public Safety Canada suggests fluid rated to -40°C and carrying a spare jug.

Before a winter drive: the UK Highway Code (rule 229) says you must clear all snow and ice from every window and keep lights clean and number plates readable. It also says to clear the mirrors, demist the windows, and remove snow that could fall onto other road users.

Add a Wiper blades reminder in Checkpit for every 6 or 12 months.

posts.title: Engine air filter: when it really needs changing
posts.body:
The engine air filter keeps dirt out of the air your engine takes in.

Fuel economy: Oak Ridge National Laboratory tests for the US Department of Energy found that on modern fuel-injected cars, a clogged filter had no measurable effect on fuel economy but did slow acceleration. With a clean filter, full-throttle 20 to 80 mph times were 6% to 11% quicker. FuelEconomy.gov says only older carbureted engines (built until the early 1980s) gain a few percent in fuel economy from a new filter.

When to change it: AAA says most makers call for regular inspection, with replacement as needed or at a set mileage. In clean city or suburban driving, a filter may last 20,000 miles (about 32,000 km) or more; dusty roads call for more frequent changes. Your owner's manual has the interval for your car.

How to check: dirt you can see doesn't always mean it's worn out. AAA's test for pleated paper filters is to hold it up to a bright light; if more than half the light gets through, it can stay in. That test doesn't work for dense fabric "extended life" filters, so change those at the maker's interval unless they're visibly caked with dirt. Some pickups have an indicator on the filter housing to check at each oil change.

Changing the filter more often than needed costs money without a real benefit.

Add an Air filter reminder in Checkpit at your manual's interval and log each change with the mileage.

Sources:
- AAA, Changing Your Car's Engine Air Filter: https://www.aaa.com/autorepair/articles/changing-your-cars-engine-air-filter
- FuelEconomy.gov, Keeping Your Vehicle in Shape: https://www.fueleconomy.gov/feg/maintain.jsp
- U.S. Department of Energy, Fact #568: For Modern Cars, Replacing an Air Filter Will Improve Performance but Not Fuel Economy: https://www.energy.gov/eere/vehicles/fact-568-april-27-2009-modern-cars-replacing-air-filter-will-improve-performance-not

posts.title: Cabin air filter: what it does and when to change it
posts.body:
The cabin air filter cleans the outside air that comes into the car through the heating, ventilation and air conditioning. AAA says it catches dust, pollen, mold, soot and insects, which can help drivers with allergies.

Types: a standard pleated filter traps most larger particles, but smaller ones such as mold spores and soot can get through. HEPA filters catch finer particles, and activated carbon filters (gray in color) also cut odors such as exhaust smells.

When to change it: AAA says carmakers' intervals range from 15,000 to 30,000 miles (about 24,000 to 48,000 km). Your owner's manual has the figure for your car. Change it sooner if you drive where there's a lot of dust or pollen.

Signs it's clogged: weak airflow from the vents, windows that fog up and are slow to clear, a smell that won't go away, and dust building up inside. A blocked filter also makes the blower fan work harder.

Doing it yourself: the filter usually sits behind the glove box, under the dashboard, or under the hood near the base of the windshield. AAA says most take under 15 minutes without tools. Fit the right size and type, and match the airflow arrows on the frame. Some cars that came without a filter still have the housing for one; the manual will say.

In wildfire smoke, the US EPA suggests closing the windows and running the air conditioning on recirculate.

Add a Cabin air filter reminder in Checkpit and log each change.

Sources:
- AAA, The Importance of Cabin Air Filter Replacement for Your Vehicle: https://www.aaa.com/autorepair/articles/changing-the-cabin-air-filter-in-your-car
- US EPA, Reduce Your Smoke Exposure: https://www.epa.gov/wildfires/reduce-your-smoke-exposure

posts.title: Worn brake pads: the signs to watch and listen for
posts.body:
Brake pads wear a little every time you stop. AAA puts the average life at about 30,000 miles (about 48,000 km), but it varies a lot with the car, the weather and how you drive. Hard braking and stop-and-go traffic wear them faster.

Sounds: AAA says a high-pitched squeal when braking often means the pads are very thin and the built-in wear indicator is touching the rotor. AA Ireland warns that grinding may mean worn pads are already damaging the discs.

Feel: a vibrating pedal (AAA says often from warped rotors), a pedal that feels soft or spongy, longer stopping distances, or a car that pulls to one side when you brake.

Other signs: a burning smell, a leak of clear-yellow oily fluid near a wheel, or a brake warning light. AA Ireland notes the brake fluid warning light can come on when the reservoir level drops.

Look: AAA suggests checking the pads through the wheel spokes. If the pad material looks thinner than about 1/4 inch (about 6 mm), it's likely time for new pads. Look for grooves or cracks on the rotor too.

AA Ireland says not to wait for your next scheduled service if you notice any of these; have the brakes inspected. AAA suggests having them checked at each tire rotation, and warns that driving on worn brakes can damage other parts and cost more to fix.

Log brake checks and pad changes in Checkpit as Brake pads, so you can see how long your last set lasted.

Sources:
- AAA, 11 Ways To Know You May Need New Brakes: https://www.aaa.com/autorepair/articles/5-ways-to-know-you-may-need-brake-repair
- AA Ireland, How to Detect Worn Brake Pads: https://www3.theaa.ie/aa/aa-membership/members-advice/driving-hints-and-tips/detecting-worn-brake-pads.aspx

posts.title: Tire rotation: how often and which pattern
posts.body:
Each wheel position wears tires differently. Front tires usually wear faster because they do the steering and much of the braking. Moving the tires around evens out the wear, so they last longer and grip more evenly.

How often: NHTSA says that if your carmaker recommends rotation, it's usually every 5,000 to 8,000 miles (about 8,000 to 13,000 km), or sooner if you see uneven wear. Advice differs: Bridgestone says every 5,000 miles, Michelin every 5,000 to 7,000 miles or every other oil change, and carmakers' own schedules vary by model. Your owner's manual comes first.

Patterns: Bridgestone and Michelin describe the usual ones. Front-wheel drive: front tires go straight back and rear tires cross to the front. Rear-wheel drive: the reverse. All-wheel and four-wheel drive: an X pattern unless the maker says otherwise. Directional tires go front to back on the same side. If the front and rear tires are different sizes, rotation may not be possible, as NHTSA notes. A full-size spare can be part of the rotation.

On all-wheel-drive cars, Bridgestone notes that even tread depth also eases strain on the drivetrain. Some tire warranties require regular rotation.

A rotation is a good time to check tire pressure, tread and damage, and AAA notes the shop can look at the brakes too.

Set a Tire rotation reminder in Checkpit to match your manual, and log each rotation.

Sources:
- NHTSA, Tire Safety Ratings and Awareness: https://www.nhtsa.gov/equipment/tires
- Michelin, Tire Rotation: Why It Matters and How to Do It: https://www.michelinman.com/auto/auto-tips-and-advice/tire-maintenance/tire-rotation
- Bridgestone Canada, Tire Rotation: How and Why to Rotate Your Tires: https://tires.bridgestone.com/en-ca/learn/automotive/tire-maintenance/tire-rotation
- AAA Via, When Should You Rotate Your Tires?: https://mwg.aaa.com/via/car/when-to-rotate-tires

posts.title: Wheel alignment: signs you need one
posts.body:
Alignment sets the angle of the wheels so the tires roll straight and sit square to the road. NHTSA says good alignment makes tires last longer and keeps the car from drifting on a straight, level road. It's a job for a qualified technician.

Signs, from AAA: the car pulls to one side on a smooth, straight road (check tire pressure first, since a low tire can do this too); the steering wheel is off-center when you drive straight; tires wear on the inside or outside edge; the tread ribs feel feathered on one side; the wheel is slow to return to center after a turn; or the steering feels loose or shimmies. A car that seems to move slightly sideways can mean collision damage.

AAA cites Goodyear: being out by 1/8 inch of toe or one degree of camber can increase wear on one edge by 20 percent. Poor alignment also adds rolling resistance, which costs fuel. Continental notes that a vibrating steering wheel alone doesn't prove misalignment; NHTSA says balancing is what prevents vibration.

When to check: AAA suggests at each tire rotation or at least once a year. Continental adds after hitting a pothole or curb, after a collision or new suspension parts, when fitting new tires, and right away if you notice signs. Wear from bad alignment can't be undone.

Continental also notes a tire warranty claim may be refused if the wear comes from alignment, so keep your service records.

Log each alignment in Checkpit as an Other service with a note, so the record is there when you need it.

Sources:
- AAA Hoosier, Seven Signs of Bad Wheel Alignment: https://www.hoosier.aaa.com/auto/seven-signs-bad-wheel-alignment

- NHTSA, Tire Safety Ratings and Awareness: https://www.nhtsa.gov/equipment/tires

posts.title: Check engine light: what it means and what to do
posts.body:
The check engine light (called the engine management light in the UK) means the car's sensors have found a possible engine or emissions problem. It doesn't tell you what the fault is; a shop has to diagnose that. The AA notes it can also flash briefly when you start the car.

Steady light: AAA says this points to an ongoing problem that can affect how the car drives or its fuel economy. First check that the fuel cap is closed tightly; if the light goes out after a few days, that was likely it. If not, book a diagnosis. The AA says that with a steady amber light and no other symptoms you can usually finish your trip, then get the car checked soon.

Flashing light: both say this is more serious and can damage the catalytic converter, an expensive repair. AAA advises easing off and heading to a shop, and if it keeps flashing for more than a minute or so, switching off and having the car towed. The AA says a red light means stop driving and call for help.

Pull over safely and switch off if the light comes with strange noises, loss of power, smoke or unusual smells.

Common causes the AA lists include oxygen sensors, a blocked diesel particulate filter, airflow sensor problems linked to the air filter, and spark plugs or ignition coils. Low oil usually has its own warning light.

In Great Britain, the AA notes an engine light that stays on is a major fault at the MOT test, so the car will fail.

Log the diagnosis and repair in Checkpit as an Other service, with the fault code in the note.

Sources:
- The AA, Engine management light: https://www.theaa.com/breakdown-cover/advice/engine-management-light
- AAA Western and Central New York, The check engine light: What to do when your dashboard signals trouble: https://westerncentralnyaaa.com/blog/check-engine-light-what-do-when-your-dashboard-signals-trouble

posts.title: Hybrid car maintenance: what's the same and what's different
posts.body:
A hybrid still has a gasoline engine, so the US Department of Energy's Alternative Fuels Data Center says hybrids and plug-in hybrids need the same general maintenance as conventional cars, so follow your owner's manual schedule for the engine, such as oil changes.

What's different: the hybrid battery, motor and electronics usually need little scheduled maintenance. Brakes generally last longer, because regenerative braking uses the motor to slow the car and recharge the battery. FuelEconomy.gov suggests anticipating stops and braking gently, since hard braking falls back on the friction brakes, which don't recover energy.

Hybrid checks: some makers offer a dedicated check. Toyota Ireland, for example, describes a yearly hybrid health check that covers a hybrid system diagnostic, hybrid battery health and insulation, the 12V auxiliary battery and the cooling system. Ask your dealer what your car's schedule includes.

Battery warranty: these vary by maker, model year and country. Toyota USA, for example, says its hybrid batteries have a 10-year/150,000-mile limited warranty, whichever comes first. Check your own warranty booklet.

Plug-in hybrids: FuelEconomy.gov says keeping the battery charged means the engine runs less. Your owner's manual has the charging advice for your car.

Log hybrid checks in Checkpit as High-voltage battery check, and keep oil change reminders as on any car.

posts.title: Electric car maintenance: what still needs looking after
posts.body:
Electric cars need less maintenance than gas cars. The US Department of Energy's Alternative Fuels Data Center says they have fewer moving parts and fluids, no engine oil to change, and a battery, motor and electronics that need little or no regular maintenance.

What still needs attention, per Consumer Reports: tires (often due for replacement around the fifth year), brake pads, the cabin air filter, the coolant (rarely changed), and suspension parts such as shock absorbers, ball joints and tie rod ends.

Brakes: regenerative braking does much of the slowing, so pads wear far less. FuelEconomy.gov suggests braking gently and anticipating stops to recover more energy.

Battery cooling: the AFDC notes some battery packs use liquid coolant that may need regular checks; your dealer or owner's manual has the schedule.

Battery warranty: the AFDC and Consumer Reports say many makers cover EV batteries for 8 years or 100,000 miles. Check your own warranty.

Safety: EVs have high-voltage systems (typically 400 to 1,000 volts, with orange cables). Leave those parts to trained technicians.

Breakdowns: AAA notes most EVs should be towed on a flatbed, and to tell roadside help you're driving an EV.

In Checkpit, set reminders for Tires, Tire rotation, Cabin air filter and Battery coolant, and log each one.

posts.title: Your electric car has a 12V battery too
posts.body:
Electric cars have two batteries. The big high-voltage pack drives the car, and a small 12-volt battery, like the one in a gas car, runs the lights, locks, windows, screens and the computers that start the car. AAA Club Alliance notes that if the 12V battery dies, the car won't start even with a full main battery.

Watch for warnings: Tesla's Model 3 manual, for example, says the owner is responsible for monitoring the low-voltage battery and that the car shows an alert when it needs replacing. It also says damage to that battery from running the car out of range isn't covered by the warranty. Check your own manual for your car's alerts.

Jump-starting: AAA says a dead 12V battery can be jumped like a gas car's. AAA Club Alliance adds: use a gas car or a portable jump pack, never another EV or a hybrid, which could badly damage both cars' electronics, and never try to jump the main battery. Find the 12V battery (often under the hood; your manual shows where), keep the clamps from touching, and drive for at least 20 minutes afterwards to recharge it.

Replacing it: use the type your maker specifies. Tesla notes some Model 3s use lead-acid and later ones lithium-ion, and warns that high-voltage parts sit nearby. If you're unsure, leave it to a shop.

A portable jump starter in the trunk can get you going without another car.

Log 12V battery tests and replacements in Checkpit as Battery.

posts.title: Before a road trip: a car checklist
posts.body:
A long drive puts hours of steady load on the car, far from your usual shop. NHTSA and the NRMA suggest these checks first.

Service: the NRMA says to look at your service sticker and book a service first if one is nearly due.

Tires: check the pressure against the recommended figure and look for uneven wear, cuts and nails. The NRMA adds the spare: make sure it's road-ready and inflated too.

Fluids: check engine oil, coolant and washer fluid and top up if needed. If you've been topping up coolant more often than usual, the NRMA says to have a technician look at it.

Battery, belts and hoses: NHTSA suggests having a mechanic test the battery and charging system, and checking belts and hoses for bulges, blisters, cracks or cuts.

Lights, wipers and brakes: walk around the car with the headlights and each indicator on. Replace wiper blades that squeak or streak. The NRMA says squealing brakes or a spongy pedal need a look before you leave.

Also from NHTSA: check the air conditioning, look up open recalls with your VIN or plate, secure any load outside the trunk, and pack a phone charger, first aid kit, flashlight, jumper cables, water and food. The NRMA adds: make sure your roadside assistance is current.

On the road, the UK Highway Code recommends a break of at least 15 minutes after every two hours of driving, and stopping somewhere safe if you feel sleepy.

Log the pre-trip check in Checkpit as an Inspection, with anything you fixed in the note.

Sources:
- NHTSA, Consumer Alert: NHTSA Offers Safety Tips for Your Great American Road Trip: https://www.nhtsa.gov/press-releases/nhtsa-offers-safety-tips-great-american-road-trip

posts.title: Why keep your car's maintenance records
posts.body:
Records help when you make a warranty claim. The FTC says the warranty company can ask for your maintenance records, and suggests keeping records of work such as oil changes, tire rotations, belt replacement, brake pads and inspections. Without them, it warns, a claim might be denied.

In the UK, the RAC says to keep the stamped service book and an itemized invoice that lists everything done, down to the grade of oil used, to show the car was serviced in line with the maker's schedule.

They also help when you sell. The FTC tells used car buyers to research repair records, and notes a vehicle history report usually won't list mechanical problems. In Great Britain, anyone can check a car's MOT history online with its number plate, including pass or fail results and the mileage recorded at each test since 2005.

What to keep for each job: the date, the mileage, what was done, the parts and fluids used, the shop's name and the receipt.

Checkpit keeps each service with its date and cost. Put the mileage, oil grade and shop in the note, and you can export all your records as a CSV file to keep a copy or share with a buyer.

Sources:

- GOV.UK, Check the MOT history of a vehicle: https://www.gov.uk/check-mot-history
- FTC, Buying a Used Car From a Dealer: https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/buying-used-car-dealer

posts.title: Does servicing outside the dealer void your warranty?
posts.body:
In the US, UK and Australia, using an independent shop for routine servicing doesn't by itself cancel a new car warranty. The conditions differ, so check your warranty booklet.

US: the FTC says you don't have to use the dealer for maintenance or repairs to keep the warranty, and it's illegal to deny coverage because someone else did the routine maintenance. Aftermarket or recycled parts don't void the warranty either. If such a part, or its installation, damages a covered part, coverage for that damage can be denied, but the maker or dealer must prove the part caused it. Work the warranty pays for can be limited to shops the maker chooses.

UK: the RAC says Block Exemption rules, kept after Brexit, mean car makers can't void the warranty because a non-franchised garage serviced the car. It must be serviced on or before the maker's intervals with the correct parts, oils and fluids.

Australia: the ACCC says a warranty typically lets you choose your repairer as long as the maker's servicing standards are met, though some require their dealers for warranty repairs. Your consumer guarantee rights apply whoever services the car.

Keep the paperwork. The FTC says the warranty company can ask for maintenance records, and the RAC suggests a stamped service book plus an itemized invoice. Extended warranties and service contracts can have their own rules, so read them.

Log each service in Checkpit with the shop's name and the parts used in the note.

Sources:
- FTC, Auto Warranties and Auto Service Contracts: https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/auto-warranties-and-auto-service-contracts

posts.title: Car safety inspections: MOT, state and provincial checks
posts.body:
Whether your car needs a regular safety inspection depends on where it's registered. Some examples follow; check the rules for your state, province or country.

Great Britain: GOV.UK says a car needs its first MOT by the third anniversary of its registration, then every year. You can test up to a month minus a day before it runs out and keep the same renewal date. Driving without a valid MOT can bring a fine of up to £1,000.

US: rules are set by each state. New York, for example, requires a safety inspection at least every 12 months, covering seat belts, brakes, steering, suspension, tires, lights, glass, wipers, horn, mirrors and fuel leaks, usually with an emissions test that includes the check engine light on most newer gas cars.

Canada: rules are provincial. In Ontario, a Safety Standards Certificate from a licensed inspection centre is needed to transfer a used vehicle (except to a spouse) or register one from outside Ontario. It's valid for 36 days and, Ontario notes, isn't a warranty of the car's condition.

Australia: rules are set by each state. In New South Wales, most light vehicles more than 5 years old need a safety inspection report (pink slip) from an authorized station before registration renewal; the renewal notice tells you.

Log each test in Checkpit as an Inspection and set the next reminder for when it's due.

Sources:
- GOV.UK, Getting an MOT: https://www.gov.uk/getting-an-mot
- New York State DMV, New York State Vehicle Safety/Emissions Inspection Program: https://dmv.ny.gov/inspection/new-york-vehicle-inspection-program-nyvip
- Government of Ontario, Safety standards certificate: https://www.ontario.ca/page/safety-standards-certificate
- Service NSW, Get a safety inspection report (pink slip): https://www.service.nsw.gov.au/transaction/esafety-checks-pink-slips

posts.title: Automatic transmission fluid: checking it and when to change it
posts.body:
In an automatic transmission, the fluid does several jobs at once. AAA says it transmits power, works the hydraulic controls, lubricates and cools the parts, and keeps the seals in good condition.

When to change it: follow your maker's schedule, which differs for normal and severe use. AAA notes many newer cars never need a change, and some "lifetime" fluids are changed only after more than 100,000 miles (about 160,000 km). The Car Care Council's general advice is a fluid and filter change every 24,000 to 36,000 miles (about 39,000 to 58,000 km) for the longest transmission life. Your owner's manual decides.

Checking the level: many newer cars have a sealed transmission with no dipstick; AAA says the level stays right as long as nothing leaks. If yours has a dipstick, AAA suggests checking monthly with the transmission warm (about 15 minutes of driving) and the engine idling, following the manual's steps, and never overfilling, which makes the fluid foam.

Color and smell: new fluid is red or pink. Reddish-amber to medium brown is normal aging. Dark brown or black means it's worn out and due for a change. Milky fluid or a burnt smell points to a bigger problem; have a mechanic look soon.

Use the right fluid: AAA says most makers have their own specification, and the wrong fluid can hurt shifting, shorten transmission life and may void the warranty.

Log each change in Checkpit as Transmission fluid and set the next reminder from your manual.

Sources:
- AAA, Automatic Transmission Fluid Service: https://www.aaa.com/autorepair/articles/automatic-transmission-fluid-service
- Car Care Council, Vehicle Systems Overview: https://www.carcare.org/vehicle-systems-overview/

posts.title: Spark plugs: how long they last and signs they're worn
posts.body:
Spark plugs make the spark that lights the fuel and air in a gasoline engine. Most cars have four; V6 and V8 engines typically have six and eight. Diesel engines have no spark plugs; they use glow plugs to help cold starts.

How long they last: AAA says most last 20,000 to 100,000 miles (about 32,000 to 160,000 km), and the RAC gives a wider 20,000 to 150,000 miles, depending on the plug and how the car is driven. Copper plugs wear out fastest; platinum and iridium last much longer. Your owner's manual gives the interval for your engine.

Signs of worn plugs, from AAA: hard starting (especially in the cold), rough idle or vibration, misfires that can turn on the check engine light, lower fuel economy, sluggish acceleration, and rattling or popping from the engine. AAA adds that worn plugs can also strain the ignition coils.

In the UK, the RAC notes plugs aren't checked at the MOT; a full service is when a mechanic looks at them. On a used car, they may be due sooner than on a new one.

Doing it yourself: the RAC says it's a fairly simple job for an experienced home mechanic. Work on a cold engine and start each new plug by hand so it doesn't cross-thread. If you're unsure, let a shop do it.

Log each change in Checkpit as Spark plugs, with the plug type in the note.

Sources:
- RAC, What are spark plugs? Maintenance and replacement guide: https://www.rac.co.uk/drive/advice/car-maintenance/what-are-spark-plugs-maintenance-and-replacement-guide/
- AAA, What is the Average Spark Plug Replacement Cost?: https://www.aaa.com/autorepair/articles/what-is-the-average-spark-plug-replacement-cost

posts.title: Timing belt or timing chain: what to know
posts.body:
The timing belt (called the cambelt in the UK) keeps the crankshaft and camshaft turning in step, so the valves open and close at the right moment. Some engines use a metal timing chain instead.

Belt or chain: the AA explains that belts are rubber and can dry out and crack with age, while chains run inside the engine in oil and generally last longer. Some engines use a "wet belt" that runs in oil and needs the correct oil grade. The RAC notes a chain can be just as expensive to replace if it does wear out. Your owner's manual says which your engine has.

When to replace a belt: intervals vary by make and model. The AA gives a common range of 40,000 to 100,000 miles (about 64,000 to 160,000 km) or 4 years, whichever comes first; the RAC says 60,000 to 100,000 miles or five to six years. Follow your manual's figure.

Why it matters: if a belt snaps, the AA says pistons can hit the valves and bend or break them, and the engine can stop while you're driving. The RAC warns many belts give no warning before they fail.

Signs to act on, from the AA and RAC: a rubbing, rattling or ticking noise from the belt area, misfires or loss of power, rough idle, trouble starting, or a cracked or frayed belt. If you hear rubbing, the AA says switch off and call a mechanic.

On many cars the belt also drives the water pump, so the AA says they're often replaced together; check the quote covers the belt, tensioners and labor.

Log a belt change in Checkpit as Timing belt and set the next reminder by distance and months.

Sources:
- The AA, What is a cam belt and when should you replace it?: https://www.theaa.com/driving-advice/service-repair/cam-belts
- RAC, What is a cambelt and how do you replace it?: https://www.rac.co.uk/drive/advice/car-maintenance/what-is-a-cambelt-and-how-do-you-replace-it/

posts.title: Serpentine (drive) belt: signs it needs replacing
posts.body:
The serpentine belt, also called the drive or accessory belt, runs from the engine to several parts at once. AAA and the RAC list the alternator, air conditioning and power steering pump, and on some engines the water pump. It's a different belt from the timing belt.

When to replace it: both AAA and the RAC put typical life at 60,000 to 100,000 miles (about 96,000 to 160,000 km); check your owner's manual. The RAC notes heat and oil contamination can make it fail early.

What to look for: cracks, fraying, or a shiny, glazed surface. AAA says to replace the belt right away if you see any of these, and to check the tension and pulley alignment too. The RAC adds overheating, steering trouble or charging faults, often with a warning light.

What to listen for, per AAA: a squeal or chirp at startup, when accelerating or when the A/C comes on usually means slipping and can wait for a service. Metallic grinding (often a failing tensioner or pulley) or slapping and knocking that changes with engine speed needs attention right away.

If it breaks: because one belt runs several systems, they can all stop at once. The RAC says that means an immediate breakdown, with the risk of overheating, battery failure and costly engine damage.

Log belt checks and replacements in Checkpit as an Other service, with "serpentine belt" in the note.

Sources:
- RAC, Serpentine belt replacement cost guide: https://www.rac.co.uk/drive/advice/car-maintenance/serpentine-belt-replacement/
- AAA Club Group, A Guide to Automotive Belts and Hoses: https://www.acg.aaa.com/connect/blogs/5c/auto/a-guide-to-automotive-belts-and-hoses

posts.title: Headlights and bulbs: checking, cleaning and aim
posts.body:
Working lights help you see and be seen. The AA suggests checking every light, including the number plate and fog lights, at least once every two weeks. Ask someone to watch, or look at the reflection in a window or a wall as you pull up close.

Clean lenses: dirt cuts light, so wipe the lights (and the windshield) regularly. AAA says years of sun can oxidize the lens coating so it turns yellow or cloudy. AAA research found restoring old headlights can double the maximum light and cut glare-causing scatter by up to 60%. The AA notes specialist products can treat clouded lenses; if cleaning doesn't help, see a shop.

Aim: lights aimed too high dazzle other drivers, and too low shorten your view. The AA says aim can shift with heavy loads, suspension problems or a hard knock from a pothole. Your owner's manual explains how to check it on level ground, or a shop can do it. AAA describes a wall test: park on level ground about 25 feet (about 7.6 m) from a wall with the low beams on; the top of each beam should sit slightly below the height of the headlight.

High beams: AAA research found they can improve how far you see by 28%. Use them on unlit roads, and dip them whenever a vehicle is coming toward you or ahead of you.

In the UK, the AA notes the MOT checks lights for condition, operation and aim, and a broken light can bring a £50 fixed penalty.

Log bulb changes or headlight restoration in Checkpit as an Other service, with the bulb type in the note.

Sources:
- The AA, Car headlights: LED, sidelights, running lights: https://www.theaa.com/driving-advice/safety/using-your-lights
- AAA Club Group, Car Headlight Safety: Tips for High Beams, Visibility & Maintenance: https://www.acg.aaa.com/connect/blogs/4c/auto/headlight-safety-tips

posts.title: Tire pressure warning light (TPMS): what to do
posts.body:
A tire pressure monitoring system (TPMS) warns you when pressure is off. AAA says US makers have had to fit it to new vehicles since 2008, and the RAC says all new cars in the UK have one by law.

Two types: a direct system has a sensor in each wheel, often on the valve. An indirect system uses the anti-lock brake sensors to compare how fast the wheels spin. Your owner's manual says which you have.

Steady light: AAA says it usually comes on when a tire is about 25% off the recommended pressure. Pull over safely and check all four tires (and the spare if it has a sensor), then add air to bring them to your car's recommended pressure. A badly low or flat tire needs a spare, an inflator or roadside help. AAA suggests rechecking a topped-up tire about a week later for a slow leak.

Flashing light: if it flashes and then stays on, both AAA and the RAC say it usually means a fault in the system itself; have it checked.

Cold mornings: cold air lowers tire pressure, so AAA notes the light may come on and go off after a few miles. Check and fill when the tires are cold.

After inflating, some cars need a reset by a button or menu; the RAC suggests following the manual, then driving about 10 minutes. Sensor batteries are sealed and usually last up to 10 years, and the RAC advises servicing valves and sensors when new tires are fitted. In the UK, a lit TPMS light fails the MOT.

TPMS doesn't replace regular checks. Log pressure checks and sensor work in Checkpit as Tires, with a note.

Sources:
- AAA Via, What Does My Car's Tire Pressure Light Mean?: https://mwg.aaa.com/via/car/tpms-light-meaning
- RAC, Tyre pressure monitoring systems (TPMS) guide: https://www.rac.co.uk/drive/advice/car-maintenance/tyre-pressure-monitoring-system-TPMS-guide/

posts.title: Car air conditioning: keeping it working
posts.body:
Your air conditioning uses refrigerant gas to cool the air, and the AA notes it also improves the air quality inside the car.

Run it regularly: the RAC says using the A/C keeps oil moving around the seals; if it sits unused, seals can dry out and refrigerant can leak. The AA suggests running it at least once a week. In winter it doubles as a demister because the air it blows is dry.

Regas and service: the AA says most makers recommend a regas every 2 years, and a full A/C service every 30,000 miles (about 48,000 km) or 2 years. Signs it's due: air from the vents isn't clearly colder than the cabin, or you can't remember the last service, for example on a used car.

Leaks: the US EPA notes topping off the refrigerant can restore cooling but doesn't fix a leak, while repairing the leak lasts longer. In the US, technicians who work on A/C refrigerant must be certified and use approved recycling equipment.

Smells: a musty smell usually comes from bacteria or mold in the system. The RAC suggests an antibacterial treatment and a new cabin air filter; the AA notes some services include this.

Do it yourself? The AA recommends a garage: refrigerant can injure skin, mixing gas types can be dangerous, and a wrong charge can damage the compressor.

Log A/C services in Checkpit as an Other service, and keep a Cabin air filter reminder.

Sources:
- The AA, Guide to air-con regassing: https://www.theaa.com/car-servicing/advice/guide-to-air-con-regassing
- RAC, Should you use your air-con in the winter?: https://www.rac.co.uk/drive/advice/car-maintenance/air-con-myths-busted/
- US EPA, Options for Recharging Your Air Conditioner: https://www.epa.gov/mvac/options-recharging-your-air-conditioner

posts.title: Shock absorbers and struts: signs they're worn
posts.body:
Shock absorbers control how each wheel moves up and down after a bump, so the car doesn't keep bouncing and the tires stay pressed to the road.

Shocks or struts: AAA Club Alliance explains that both damp bumps, but a strut is also a structural part that carries the car's weight and helps keep the wheels aligned. Many cars use struts at the front and shocks at the rear; your owner's manual says which you have, and one can't replace the other.

How long they last: the RAC puts it at roughly 50,000 to 100,000 miles (about 80,000 to 160,000 km), depending on the car, the parts and how it's driven and stored.

Signs of wear, from the RAC: the car feels less stable or handles poorly, more vibration or noise over bumps, longer stopping distances, a car that sits lower than before, fluid leaking from a shock, and rust or corrosion on it. Cars with adaptive or air suspension may show a warning light. Worn shocks also make tires wear faster.

Replace them in pairs, both front or both rear, so the two sides behave the same, the RAC advises.

A passed inspection isn't a guarantee: DVSA notes an MOT certificate only reflects the car on the day of the test, and keeping it roadworthy is the owner's job.

Log suspension checks and shock or strut replacements in Checkpit as an Other service, with the axle in the note.

Sources:
- RAC, Shock absorber replacement cost guide: https://www.rac.co.uk/drive/advice/car-maintenance/shock-absorber-replacement-cost-and-maintenance-guide/
- AAA Club Alliance, What's The Difference Between Shocks and Struts: https://cluballiance.aaa.com/the-extra-mile/advice/car/what-is-the-difference-between-shocks-and-struts
- DVSA, Matters of Testing, Why was the shock absorber bounce test removed from the MOT test?: https://mattersoftesting.blog.gov.uk/your-questions-answered-why-were-shock-absorbers-removed-from-the-mot-test/

posts.title: Gas octane: regular or premium?
posts.body:
The octane number shows how well gasoline resists engine knock. In the US, FuelEconomy.gov says regular is usually 87, midgrade 88 to 90 and premium 91 to 94.

What your car needs: check the owner's manual. Most cars are designed for 87. AAA's 2016 fact sheet says about 70% of drivers own a vehicle that needs regular, 16% one that needs premium and 10% midgrade.

"Required" or "recommended": if premium is required, use it. FuelEconomy.gov says lower octane can make the engine run poorly, may damage the engine and emissions system over time and may void the warranty; newer cars adjust the timing to protect the engine, so you lose power and fuel economy. If premium is only recommended, it's your choice; the extra cost usually outweighs any savings.

Premium in a car built for regular: little or no benefit in normal driving. In AAA's tests it gave no gain in horsepower, fuel economy or emissions. AAA estimated 16.5 million Americans used premium they didn't need in 12 months, spending more than $2.1 billion.

If you want better fuel, AAA suggests a TOP TIER gasoline instead of a higher octane; in its tests, gas that wasn't TOP TIER left 19 times more engine deposits. At high altitude, 85 octane is meant only for older carbureted engines, FuelEconomy.gov says.

Log fill-ups in Checkpit and put the grade in the fuel Note, so you can compare economy between grades.

Sources:
- FuelEconomy.gov, Selecting the Right Octane Fuel: https://www.fueleconomy.gov/feg/octane.shtml
- AAA, Premium Fuel Fact Sheet: https://newsroom.aaa.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/09/Premium-Fuel-Fact-Sheet-FINAL.pdf

posts.title: Road salt and rust: protecting your car in winter
posts.body:
Salt keeps winter roads safer, but salty water speeds up rust. AAA says the underside takes the most: seams, axle housings and wheel wells. Salt also holds moisture. AAA cites an EPA estimate of $5 billion a year in road salt damage to vehicles.

Wash often: AAA suggests washing about every two weeks in winter, more after heavy snow, and always including the underside. Consumer Reports says an underbody wash is worth it at least once a season, especially after mud or salted roads, and that a high-pressure wash only works as well as its water pressure. AAA also suggests a rinse with plain water after driving on heavily salted roads.

Wax and parking: AAA says wax slows corrosion but doesn't stop it, and parking in a garage helps. Consumer Reports calls spray-on wax at a car wash mostly cosmetic.

Check for damage: look under the car, in the wheel wells, along the frame and at the edges of the doors, hood and trunk for bubbling paint. AAA also mentions gaskets, seals and wiring. Warning signs: a louder engine can mean a muffler or exhaust that has rusted through, and squeaks over bumps can mean damaged bushings. Consumer Reports notes rust starts where the protective layer is broken or where salt, mud or sand gets trapped.

Log washes in Checkpit as an expense with the Car wash category, so you can see how often you washed this winter.

Sources:
- AAA Club Group, Protecting Your Car from Road Salt Damage: https://www.acg.aaa.com/connect/blogs/6c/auto/protecting-your-car-from-road-salt-damage
- Consumer Reports, Are Car-Wash Extras Worth It?: https://www.consumerreports.org/cars/car-maintenance/should-you-pay-more-for-a-car-wash-a3449806636/

posts.title: Fluid under your car: what the color tells you
posts.body:
A puddle under the car can be harmless water or a sign of a serious fault. To check, the RAC suggests leaving white cardboard under the car overnight; note the color, smell and where the drip is, and make sure it's coming from your car.

Clear water with no smell, near the front passenger side, is usually condensation from the air conditioning. Both the RAC and AAA say it's normal.

Blue, green, purple, yellow or orange with a glass-cleaner smell, at the front, is usually washer fluid, AAA says. Coolant can also be green, yellow, pink, blue or clear but smells sweet; the RAC says have it checked soon and avoid long trips.

Brown, black or amber and greasy, under the engine, is usually engine oil. AAA says a small amount can be normal; the RAC says drive as little as possible and see a garage soon.

Red, pink or reddish-brown in the middle or front of the car can be transmission fluid, which both rate as urgent; the RAC suggests not driving and getting a tow. Power steering fluid looks similar, near the front or the steering hoses; AAA says it smells like burnt marshmallows and rates it very urgent.

Slippery fluid near a wheel that is clear, yellowish or light brown can be brake fluid. Both rate it the most serious: don't drive, get a tow. A rainbow sheen and a strong fuel smell, often at the rear, means fuel; the RAC says don't drive.

Log the repair in Checkpit under the matching service type, such as Coolant, Transmission fluid or Brake fluid, or Other with a note on what leaked.

Sources:
- RAC, Car leaking? How to identify liquid dripping from your car and what to do: https://www.rac.co.uk/drive/advice/know-how/car-leaking-how-to-identify-liquid-dripping-from-your-car-and-what-to-do/
- AAA Club Group, What is Leaking from Your Car: The Ultimate Guide to Automotive Leaks: https://www.acg.aaa.com/connect/blogs/4c/auto/guide-to-automotive-leaks

posts.title: Jump-starting a car safely
posts.body:
Before you start: check both batteries. The AA and RAC say not to jump a battery that is leaking, cracked or badly corroded, or to use damaged leads. Both cars should use the same voltage, usually 12 V. Use a hybrid or EV as the donor only if its manual allows it; the AA advises against it. Remove jewelry, don't smoke, and follow your owner's manual.

Set up: park the cars close but not touching, set both parking brakes, and switch off both ignitions and electrics like lights and radio.

Connect, per the AA and RAC: red lead to the positive (+) terminal of both batteries, then black lead to the negative (-) terminal of the working battery, and the other black end to bare, unpainted metal on the dead car, away from the battery and fuel system. Never let the clamps touch each other.

Start: run the donor car for a few minutes, then try the dead car. The RAC suggests cranking no more than about 5 seconds at a time. Once it runs, the AA suggests letting both cars run for about 10 minutes.

Disconnect in reverse order: black from the dead car's metal first, then black from the donor, then the red leads. Keep the leads away from fans and belts.

Afterward, drive for at least 30 minutes, ideally not in stop-start traffic, so the battery can recharge. A charged jump pack works without a second car; follow its instructions.

Log battery tests or a replacement in Checkpit as Battery, with a note about the jump start.

Sources:
- The AA, How to jump start a car in 9 steps: https://www.theaa.com/breakdown-cover/advice/using-jump-leads
- RAC, How to jump start a car in 10 steps (with video): https://www.rac.co.uk/drive/advice/car-maintenance/how-to-jump-start-a-car/
