posts.title: Spare tire or repair kit: know what your car has
posts.body:
Many new cars no longer carry a spare. AAA found 28% of 2017 models lacked one as standard, as makers cut weight to improve fuel economy, and the AA estimates the vast majority of new cars in the UK don't have one as standard.

Check before you need it: look under the trunk floor and in your owner's manual. When buying a new car, AAA suggests asking whether a spare is included or can be added, and the AA suggests choosing the spare option where practical.

Inflator kits: AAA says they can temporarily fix small punctures but not sidewall damage or blowouts, and the sealant has a shelf life of about four to eight years, so check the expiry date and read the manual for the kit's limits. The AA says a kit can fail to seal the tire, and more than half of the punctured cars its patrols attended in a year had no spare.

Space-saver spares: the AA says they're usually limited to 50 mph (about 80 km/h); check the label and handbook. They have only 3 mm of tread from new and softer rubber, so don't go far, and some can only be fitted at the front or rear. Get the original tire repaired or replaced as soon as possible.

Keep it ready: AAA suggests checking the pressure of all five tires monthly. With no spare, the AA suggests a plan, like saving a mobile tire fitter's number and your tire size in your phone; AAA also mentions roadside assistance cover.

Log tire repairs and spare checks in Checkpit as Tires, with the kit's expiry date in the note.

Sources:
- AAA Oregon/Idaho, Spare me! AAA Finds One-Third of New Vehicles don't have Spare Tire: https://info.oregon.aaa.com/spare-me-aaa-finds-one-third-of-new-vehicles-dont-have-spare-tire/
- The AA, Four-fifths prefer a spare: https://www.theaa.com/about-us/newsroom/four-fifths-prefer-a-spare
- The AA, Spare wheels: https://www.theaa.com/driving-advice/safety/non-standard-spare-wheels

posts.title: Power steering: fluid, electric systems and warning signs
posts.body:
Power steering cuts the effort needed to turn the wheel, especially at low speeds like parking, AAA explains. The RAC says hydraulic systems use a pump, fluid and a reservoir, while electric power steering (EPS), found in many modern cars, has no pump or fluid reservoir. Your owner's manual says which you have.

Hydraulic fluid: AAA suggests checking the reservoir for level and contamination. Fresh fluid is clear with a pink or amber tint; brown or black means the system should be flushed and refilled. Use the fluid type in your owner's manual and add it slowly, since overfilling can build pressure and damage the seals.

Warning signs, from AAA: whining, groaning or grinding when turning at low speed can mean low or dirty fluid, a squeal at startup can point to a worn belt, and stiff steering at low speed or pink or amber fluid under the car near the reservoir or hoses need a check. The RAC adds that a broken drive belt stops the pump and can affect charging and cooling too.

Electric systems: a Kia owner's manual says that if EPS stops working, you can still steer but it takes more effort, and a warning light comes on. It lists as normal a heavier feel right after start during a self-check, and heavier steering or noise in the cold that fades as it warms up.

Warning light: the RAC says don't ignore it and recommends not driving until the fault is checked, because the car can become hard to steer.

Log power steering work in Checkpit as an Other service, with "power steering" in the note.

Sources:
- AAA Club Alliance, Warning Signs of a Power Steering Leak: https://cluballiance.aaa.com/the-extra-mile/advice/car/warning-signs-of-a-power-steering-leak
- RAC, Power steering warning light: https://www.rac.co.uk/drive/advice/car-maintenance/power-steering-warning-light/
- Kia Owner's Manual, Electric Power Steering (EPS): https://ownersmanual.kia.com/docview/webhelp/doc/98e02d4b-7e6f-483a-99b0-ae80598a8edf/topics/chapter5_10_1.html

posts.title: Diesel exhaust fluid (DEF/AdBlue): what diesel drivers need to know
posts.body:
Many newer diesels clean their exhaust with selective catalytic reduction (SCR), which needs diesel exhaust fluid (DEF), sold in Europe as AdBlue. The AA says it's a colorless, non-toxic mix of 32.5% urea and 67.5% deionized water. It's sprayed into the exhaust, where it helps turn nitrogen oxides (NOx) into nitrogen and water vapor. The US EPA says nearly all on-road diesel trucks have used DEF since 2010.

Does your car use it? The AA says check the handbook, look for a blue filler cap, or look for "Blue" or "SCR" in the model name.

How much: the AA gives about 1 liter every 600 miles (about 970 km), and up to 1 liter every 350 miles (about 560 km). Tanks need refilling every 3,000 to 12,000 miles (about 4,800 to 19,000 km), so most drivers top up at least once between services.

Running low: a dashboard warning with a countdown typically appears about 1,500 miles (about 2,400 km) before empty, the AA says. If the tank runs dry, power drops and the engine won't restart once stopped. The EPA notes these systems can limit speed to as low as 5 mph or stop the vehicle working, and has urged makers to offer software updates that ease those limits. The AA suggests adding about 5 liters to restart; the warning usually clears after a top-up, sometimes after a short drive.

Topping up: never put DEF in the fuel tank or diesel in the DEF tank. The AA says if it happens, don't switch on the ignition; the tank has to be drained, and the mistake can cause expensive damage. Rinse spills, since DEF can irritate skin and eyes, damage paint and crystallize on carpets.

Log top-ups in Checkpit as DEF / AdBlue and set a distance reminder for the next one.

Sources:
- The AA, What is AdBlue?: https://www.theaa.com/breakdown-cover/advice/adblue
- US EPA, Diesel Exhaust Fluid: https://www.epa.gov/regulations-emissions-vehicles-and-engines/diesel-exhaust-fluid

posts.title: Diesel particulate filter (DPF): keeping it clear
posts.body:
Most modern diesel cars have a diesel particulate filter (DPF) in the exhaust. It traps soot so it doesn't come out of the tailpipe. GOV.UK notes these filters help meet European emission standards. Because the filter can only hold so much, the soot has to be burned off, which is called regeneration.

How it cleans itself, per the RAC: on a long run at steady speed, the soot can burn off on its own. When the filter gets about 45% full, the engine also starts an active cycle by adding extra fuel. Signs one is running include a changed engine note, cooling fans running, a higher idle and Stop/Start switching off. If a short trip interrupts it, the RAC suggests about 10 minutes at over 40 mph (about 65 km/h) to let it finish.

What blocks it: mostly short, slow trips. The RAC also lists poor servicing, the wrong engine oil (DPF cars usually need low-ash "low-SAPS" oil), low-quality fuel, modifications and often running on a near-empty tank. It suggests a regular 30 to 50 minute run at steady speed on a highway.

Warning light: an orange DPF light means the filter is clogged or there's a fault. If it goes out after a long drive, nothing more is needed. If it stays on, turns red, or the car loses power, have a garage check it soon; a red light means stop as soon as it's safe.

Don't remove it: GOV.UK says driving a car with its standard DPF taken out is an offence in the UK, and it fails the MOT, which has checked for the filter since February 2014.

Log DPF cleaning or repairs in Checkpit as an Other service, and note the oil type when you log an Oil change.

Sources:
- RAC, Diesel particulate filters: guide to DPFs: https://www.rac.co.uk/drive/advice/car-maintenance/diesel-particulate-filters/
- GOV.UK, New rules for MOT to test for diesel particulate filter: https://www.gov.uk/government/news/new-rules-for-mot-to-test-for-diesel-particulate-filter

posts.title: "Severe" driving conditions: which maintenance schedule fits you
posts.body:
Many owner's manuals give two maintenance schedules: a normal one and a stricter one for severe or special conditions. AAA says to follow the stricter schedule if your driving fits it.

What counts as severe, per AAA: mostly short trips of 5 miles (about 8 km) or less; very hot, cold or dusty climates; long stretches of stop-and-go traffic; and carrying heavy loads or towing a trailer. Many everyday commutes fit at least one of these, so check honestly.

What changes: it depends on the car. As an example, Toyota's 2008 RAV4 maintenance guide adds extra checks for driving on dirt or dusty roads, such as the engine air filter, drive shaft boots and steering linkage. For towing, it adds earlier fluid changes, like differential and transfer case oil on 4WD models. It also says heavy traffic and dusty areas can shorten the cabin air filter's life.

Oil-life monitors: AAA says most newer cars have one that alerts you when an oil change is due and shortens the interval when it detects heavy use, which is why some newer manuals no longer print a separate severe schedule. AAA adds that these monitors aren't always accurate, so your manual's schedule comes first.

Bottom line: read your owner's manual, decide which schedule matches how you really drive, and stick to it.

Set reminders in Checkpit by distance and months using the schedule that fits your driving.

Sources:
- AAA, How Often Should You Change Your Oil?: https://www.aaa.com/autorepair/articles/how-often-should-you-change-your-oil
- Toyota, 2008 RAV4 Scheduled Maintenance Guide: https://assets.sia.toyota.com/publications/en/omms-s/T-MMS-08RAV4/pdf/T-MMS-08RAV4.pdf

posts.title: Winter tires vs all-season tires: what's the difference
posts.body:
Below about 7°C (45°F), all-season and summer tires start to lose elasticity and grip, Transport Canada says, while winter tires stay flexible at much lower temperatures. The RAC says winter tires use a softer rubber with deeper grooves and many small cuts (sipes) to clear water and snow.

The symbol: look for the peaked mountain with a snowflake. Transport Canada says tires with it have passed a snow traction test, at least 10% better than a reference tire on packed snow. There's no government standard for grip on ice in Canada, the US or the EU.

Does it matter? In a test the RAC cites, winter tires stopped in 65.7 m versus 70.5 m for summer tires at 5°C, but took slightly longer at 20°C. On snow the gap widens a lot. Transport Canada notes that after Quebec updated its winter tire rules in 2013, winter collisions there fell 19% against the previous five-year average.

Fitting them: Transport Canada says fit them in sets of four of the same type and size, and don't use tires worn close to 4 mm (5/32 in) on snowy roads. Cold weather lowers tire pressure, so check it when the tires are cold.

Rules: Quebec is the only Canadian province that requires winter tires province-wide in the winter season; other places set their own rules. The UK doesn't require them. Some insurers offer a discount, and the RAC suggests telling your insurer.

Log seasonal tire changes in Checkpit as Tires, and set a months-based reminder for the next swap.

Sources:
- Transport Canada, Using winter tires: https://tc.canada.ca/en/road-transportation/stay-safe-when-driving/winter-driving/using-winter-tires
- Transport Canada, Winter Tires (briefing note): https://tc.canada.ca/en/corporate-services/transparency/briefing-documents-transport-canada/20191120/20191120/winter-tires
- RAC, Should I buy winter tyres?: https://www.rac.co.uk/drive/advice/winter-driving/should-i-buy-winter-tyres/

posts.title: Checking a used car's service history before you buy
posts.body:
A car's service history shows how it was looked after. The AA says buyers usually want to see the full history, and it can make a big difference to the car's value.

Ask for the records: the service book is the easiest place to start, the AA says. Each stamped entry shows the date and mileage. Some makers use a digital service record instead; a dealer or the manufacturer can look it up with the car's 17-character VIN. Consumer Reports says an organized stack of repair and maintenance receipts usually means the car was cared for.

Check them: Consumer Reports suggests comparing the records with the maker's maintenance schedule and asking for receipts for replaced parts. Receipts usually list the odometer reading, which helps confirm the mileage. Be wary of a private seller who says they did all the work but has no receipts. In the UK, the AA points to the GOV.UK MOT history checker, which shows past test results.

Get a history report: the FTC recommends a vehicle history report before buying. In the US, vehiclehistory.gov lists approved providers, and NHTSA lists open recalls by VIN for free.

Get it inspected: both the FTC and Consumer Reports say a history report is no substitute for an independent inspection. Consumer Reports puts a pre-purchase check at about $100 to $150 and suggests asking for a written report.

When you sell, a Checkpit CSV export (All records) gives buyers your fuel, service and expense history in one file.

Sources:
- The AA, How can you check a car's service history?: https://www.theaa.com/car-servicing/advice/how-can-you-check-a-cars-service-history
- Consumer Reports, Used Car Checklist to Avoid Costly Repairs: https://www.consumerreports.org/cars/how-to-inspect-a-used-car-a1377126659/
- FTC, Used Cars: https://consumer.ftc.gov/features/feature-0040-used-cars

posts.title: Storing your car for a long time: what to do first
posts.body:
A car that sits for weeks or months can come back with a flat battery, flat-spotted tires or stale fuel. AAA splits its advice by length: some steps for any long stop, and more if the car will sit for over 45 days.

Before you park it: if an oil change, brake fluid or coolant change is nearly due, AAA says do it first, since old oil and fluids carry contaminants that can cause rust and corrosion. Add a fuel stabilizer, fill the tank to reduce condensation, and drive 5 to 10 miles (about 8 to 16 km) so the stabilizer reaches the fuel system.

Battery and tires: AAA suggests a maintenance charger (trickle charger) left connected to keep the battery full, with clean, tight terminals. Add about 10 psi to each tire to reduce flat spots, or move the car now and then.

Brakes and wipers: AAA advises against the parking brake, which can stick. Leave an automatic in Park, or a manual in first or reverse with wheel chocks. Lift the wiper arms off the glass so the blades don't stick.

Over 45 days: wash and dry the car, store it somewhere cool, dark and dry, or use a breathable cover, and block the tailpipe and air intake against rodents with steel or copper wool. Write a list of everything you did and leave it in the car so you undo each step before driving.

Insurance and registration: AAA says to keep the car insured in the US. In the UK, a car taken off the road needs a SORN, it must stay off public roads, and it can only be driven to a pre-booked MOT. Rules differ elsewhere, so check with your licensing office and insurer.

Log the pre-storage oil change in Checkpit, and put your storage list in the record's Note.

Sources:
- AAA, Tips for Parking and Storing Your Car for Extended Periods: https://mwg.aaa.com/via/car/parked-car-storage-tips
- GOV.UK, When you need to make a SORN: https://www.gov.uk/sorn-statutory-off-road-notification

posts.title: Exhaust system and catalytic converter: signs of trouble
posts.body:
The exhaust system carries hot gases away from the engine, quiets engine noise and helps keep carbon monoxide out of the cabin, AAA Club Alliance explains. The catalytic converter, part of the exhaust, cuts harmful emissions; the EPA calls it the most important pollution control device on a car.

Signs of a leak, per AAA: the engine sounds louder or different than usual, fuel economy drops, or you smell exhaust or fuel inside the car. A leak can let outside air reach the oxygen sensor, so the engine may add fuel it doesn't need.

Why it matters: exhaust leaking into the cabin can cause carbon monoxide poisoning, which AAA calls the most serious symptom. Have a leak checked and repaired soon, even if the car still runs normally.

Catalytic converter: the EPA says an original converter is designed to last the life of the car if the car is used and maintained properly, and that poor tuning and maintenance can ruin it. Keeping the engine in good tune is one of the best ways to protect it. For 1995 and newer cars, the EPA lists a manufacturer warranty of 8 years or 80,000 miles on the converter.

If it needs replacing: in the US, the EPA sets rules on when an aftermarket converter can be used, and it must suit your exact car. Ask the shop for an invoice that shows the reason for replacement, and check your state's emissions rules.

Log exhaust and converter repairs in Checkpit as Other, with the shop's diagnosis in the Note.

Sources:
- AAA Club Alliance, Signs Of An Exhaust Leak: https://cluballiance.aaa.com/the-extra-mile/advice/car/signs-of-an-exhaust-leak
- EPA, What You Should Know About Using, Installing, or Buying Aftermarket Catalytic Converters: https://archive.epa.gov/region02/auto/web/pdf/catcvrts.pdf

posts.title: Driving on snow and ice: slow, gentle and further back
posts.body:
The Highway Code says stopping distances in icy and snowy weather can be ten times greater than on dry roads. Its first advice is to check the forecast and only drive if the trip is essential.

Before you go: clear snow and ice from every window, the lights, mirrors and plates, and remove snow that could fall onto other road users (Highway Code rule 229). NHTSA adds that tire pressure drops with temperature, so set it to the figure your car's maker gives, not the one on the tire.

On the road: drive slowly in as high a gear as you can, and accelerate, brake and steer gently. Slow down before a bend, not in it. Leave much more room to the car in front. If steering feels light or the tires go quiet, the road may be icy (rule 231). Stay cautious even on gritted roads, and don't crowd or pass a snowplow unless the lane is clear.

Braking: NHTSA says with anti-lock brakes (ABS), press firmly and hold; without ABS, pump the brakes if the wheels start to lock. In a skid, the National Weather Service says not to brake and to steer the front wheels in the direction of the skid.

If you get stuck: NHTSA says stay with your car, keep the exhaust pipe clear of snow, and run the engine only now and then to keep warm, because of carbon monoxide.

Log your winter tire change in Checkpit as Tires, and set a months-based reminder for the spring swap.

Sources:
- GOV.UK, The Highway Code: Driving in adverse weather conditions (226 to 237): https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-highway-code/driving-in-adverse-weather-conditions-226-to-237
- NHTSA, Winter Weather Driving Tips: https://www.nhtsa.gov/winter-driving-tips
- National Weather Service, Southern Plains Winter Preparedness: https://www.weather.gov/ama/winterprep-driving

posts.title: Buying a used car: a step-by-step checklist
posts.body:
Budget for the full cost, not just the price: the FTC lists registration, insurance, fuel and maintenance. It also suggests getting out-the-door prices in writing and checking the dealer's complaint record with your state or local consumer agency.

Read the paperwork: in the US, dealers must show a Buyers Guide on each used car saying whether it's sold "as is" or with a warranty, the FTC says. In the UK, Citizens Advice says never buy without the original V5C log book, and to use the free DVLA vehicle checker to confirm the make, model and MOT details match.

Check the history: the FTC suggests a vehicle history report, which can show accidents or flood damage but usually not mechanical problems, plus a free recall check by VIN. Citizens Advice suggests a paid check (up to £20) for outstanding finance, theft or a past write-off, and checking the MOT history for gaps.

Test drive and inspect: Citizens Advice suggests viewing in daylight, driving for at least 15 minutes on different roads, and being insured for the drive. The FTC recommends an independent mechanic's inspection even on a certified car, with a written report you can use to negotiate.

Before you sign: compare financing on the total cost, not just the monthly payment, and get any return policy in writing. The FTC notes US federal law gives no automatic three-day right to cancel. Rights vary by country and state, so check with your consumer protection agency.

After you buy, add the car in Checkpit and log the inspection as Inspection, with the report's findings in the Note.

Sources:
- FTC, Buying a Used Car From a Dealer: https://www.bulkorder.ftc.gov/sites/bulkorder.ftc.gov/files/publications/539a_buying_a_used_car_en_aug2023_508.pdf
- Citizens Advice, Buying a used car: https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/consumer/cars-and-other-vehicles/buying-a-car/buying-a-used-car/what-to-watch-out-for-when-buying-a-used-car/how-to-check-a-car-s-history/
